lead: Make a forensic copy of a drive, a folder or a memory dump from a simple Windows program. It also lets you open the copy afterwards and look inside without changing it.
use_when: You need a disk image of a drive that is attached to a Windows computer.
You want to preview a drive or an image before deciding what to do with it.
You need to save only chosen files and folders in a protected image.
You want a hash report to show that the copy matches the source.

features.title: Creates images
items: Images physical and logical drives, CDs and DVDs, USB devices, folders and single files
Writes Raw (dd), SMART, E01 and AFF images
Can split an image into fragments of a size you choose
Asks for case number, evidence number, description, examiner and notes in some versions

features.title: Checks the copy
items: Calculates MD5 and SHA1 hashes while it works
A verify option compares the hashes of the drive and the image
Saves a text log next to the image with the drive details, hashes, start and end times and verification result

features.title: Looks inside evidence
items: Add Evidence Item loads an image and shows its folders, including deleted data
Image Mounting shows an image as a drive in read-only mode
Export Files copies chosen files and folders out of an image

features.title: Memory and protected data
items: Capture Memory saves the memory of a running computer to a file
Obtain Protected Files recovers files such as registry files that are locked on a live system
Can detect files encrypted with EFS
Custom content images can be encrypted with a password

requirements: It is a Windows program. Download it from the vendor, Exterro, and install or run it on the computer that the evidence drive is attached to. You need enough free space at the destination for the image, and you should use a write blocker for the source drive.

steps.title: Get the program
steps.text: Download FTK Imager from the vendor page (see the link in the Learn section) and install it on a Windows computer. Check that the destination drive has more free space than the source drive holds.

steps.title: Protect the source
steps.text: Attach the evidence drive through a write blocker. A guide from SANS notes that the program does not promise to avoid writing to a drive, so a blocker is recommended. Note the make, model and serial number of the drive.

steps.title: Start a new image
steps.text: Open the File menu and choose Create Disk Image. Pick the type of source, for example a physical drive, then choose the drive.

steps.title: Choose the image type and destination
steps.text: Click Add and pick the image type: Raw (dd), SMART, E01 or AFF. Fill in the case details if asked. Choose the destination folder and file name. Set a fragment size if you want split files, then click Finish.

steps.title: Turn on verification
steps.text: Tick the option to verify images after they are created, so the program calculates the hashes. Click Start and wait for the progress window to close. Large drives can take hours.

steps.title: Check the result
steps.text: When it finishes, read the hash results and any bad sector report. Open the text log saved next to the image and keep it with the case notes. Record the hash values in your own notes as well.

steps.title: Look inside the image
steps.text: Use File, then Add Evidence Item to load the image and browse its folders. Use Export Files to copy out items you need. Always work from a copy of the image, not the only original.

options.what: Starts the imaging wizard for a drive, CD, DVD or folder.
Saves the memory of the running computer to a file in a folder you choose.
Loads an image or drive so you can browse it.
Mounts an image so Windows shows it as a drive.
Copies files and folders out of an image.
Recovers protected files such as registry files from a live system.

cases.title: Seized laptops and desktop computers
cases.why: A drive attached through a write blocker can be imaged and hashed, and the image can then be opened in an analysis tool.

cases.title: Quick checks at the scene
cases.why: You can preview a drive and browse its files before deciding whether a full image is needed.

cases.title: USB sticks, memory cards and optical discs
cases.why: Small removable media can be imaged with the same wizard and checked with the same hash report.

cases.title: Targeted collection of files
cases.why: A custom content image saves only chosen files or folders and can be protected with a password.

cases.title: Live computers
cases.why: Memory capture and protected file collection let you save data that is lost when the computer is switched off.

strengths: Simple graphical wizard that students can learn in one session.
Writes several common image formats, so other tools can open the result.
Hashing, verification and a log file are part of the normal imaging flow.
Free to download from the vendor.
limits: It is free but closed source. You cannot read or change its code.
It runs on Windows. Linux and macOS users need a different imaging tool.
It does not stop writes to the source drive by itself. Use a write blocker.
It images and previews. Deep analysis such as timelines and keyword indexing needs another tool.
Menu names and options can differ between versions, so check the version you have.
The vendor's own pages say little about technical details. Learn from the user guide and test the tool yourself.
